section_summary: This section follows negotiations over Japan’s 1934 Petroleum Industry Law, especially oil import quotas, compulsory reserves, prices, and the future of foreign oil companies. It includes company proposals and supporting exhibits, embassy reports of talks with Japanese officials and refiners, and April telegrams reporting a provisional understanding. Separate documents concern Colombian oil inquiries, a proposed Japanese purchase of a Java oil concession, and correspondence about the reserve requirement.

people.name: Yoshino
people.role: Japanese Vice Minister of Commerce and Industry

people.name: Hashimoto
people.role: President of the Nippon Oil Company

people.name: Stanley K. Hornbeck
people.role: Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

people.name: Godber
people.role: Representative of the Shell oil interests

people.name: Shigemitsu
people.role: Host of a luncheon for oil representatives

people.name: Prioleau
people.role: Recipient of a requested message at Netherlands Koloniale Petroleum Maatschappij

subfiles.title: Continuation of memorandum of conversation with Kurusu
subfiles.about: Kurusu explains Yoshino’s position on negotiations, stock keeping, prices, and import quotas.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu says Yoshino will seek agreement from other officials without committing himself in writing beforehand. He proposes asking Japanese oil interests whether they too want stock requirements reduced and says importers should retain quotas and share in future growth.

subfiles.title: Conversation between Neville and Kurusu
subfiles.about: Kurusu urges foreign and Japanese oil companies to cooperate on reducing storage requirements.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu reports that Hashimoto sought relief from storage requirements and that Yoshino suggested a joint petition. He assures Neville that cooperation with Japanese firms would not undo earlier talks.

subfiles.title: Japanese inquiries about Colombian crude oil
subfiles.from: John Brandt, American Vice Consul, Cartagena
subfiles.about: A Japanese representative reportedly asks about Colombian crude exports and naval bunker fuel.
subfiles.summary: Brandt reports the inquiries and circulates the information to other United States officials.

subfiles.title: May forwards oil negotiation memoranda
subfiles.from: A. G. May, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: May sends conversation memoranda and attachments concerning the Petroleum Industry Control Law.
subfiles.summary: May forwards materials promised to Hornbeck by Coe.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation, February 25
subfiles.about: Kurusu discusses the foreign oil companies’ proposed memorandum with Neville and Sansom.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu objects to a preamble committing Yoshino to the companies’ proposals before consulting colleagues. He promises that their memorandum will guide further talks and outlines a possible joint approach to stock keeping, price control, and quotas.

subfiles.title: Oil companies’ letter to the Minister of Commerce and Industry
subfiles.from: Standard-Vacuum Oil Company and Rising Sun Petroleum Company
subfiles.to: Chūji Machida, Minister of Commerce and Industry
subfiles.about: The foreign companies propose a division of future gasoline sales between refiners and importers.
subfiles.summary: The companies describe their former share of Japan’s gasoline market and argue for protection against discrimination. They propose giving existing refiners the first increment of demand needed to fill spare capacity, then dividing later growth equally between refiners and importers.

subfiles.title: Cancelled preamble to petroleum memorandum
subfiles.about: A proposed preamble says Yoshino agrees with the companies’ conclusions.
subfiles.summary: The page records a preamble cancelled at officials’ request on February 23.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of matters discussed with the Ministry of Commerce
subfiles.from: Standard-Vacuum Oil Company and Rising Sun Petroleum Company
subfiles.about: The companies set out proposed understandings on quotas, reserves, refineries, prices, and business tenure.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum seeks protection of existing trade in Japan, Korea, and Taiwan and a share of future gasoline demand. It addresses newcomers, declining sales, substitution between products, and the counting of stocks in transit. It also calls for limits on refinery expansion, a price formula allowing fair profit, and licenses lasting at least ten years. Pages 166 and 168 repeat portions of adjacent pages.

subfiles.title: Exhibit A: Stock-keeping
subfiles.about: The exhibit estimates the cost of a six-month reserve requirement.
subfiles.summary: It estimates large initial, annual capital, and carrying costs and argues that reserves beyond three months have no ordinary commercial purpose.

subfiles.title: Exhibit B: Price formula and explanatory questions
subfiles.about: The exhibit proposes a cost-based formula for refined products and crude oil.
subfiles.summary: The formula includes origin prices, freight, losses, taxes, operating costs, duties, financing, insurance, and profit. An accompanying page asks how officials will define origins, allocate crude duty, and reconcile refined-product and crude-based prices.

subfiles.title: Exhibit C: Reasons for higher gasoline prices
subfiles.about: The companies argue that prevailing gasoline prices are too low.
subfiles.summary: The exhibit recounts cartel arrangements, Russian gasoline competition, and government involvement in gasoline prices. It compares prices with changes in exchange rates, tariffs, crude costs, and freight, then urges adoption of the proposed price formula.

subfiles.title: Forecast of Japan’s petroleum consumption and refining needs
subfiles.about: The memorandum projects petroleum demand and the costs of domestic refining and compulsory reserves.
subfiles.summary: Using projected demand, it estimates crude requirements, new refinery investment, and possible loss of customs revenue if imports shift from refined products to crude. It also calculates the capital needed to hold extensive crude and product reserves. The companies argue for balancing imports with local refining and limiting compulsory stocks to three months.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Standard-Vacuum
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges material about Japan’s oil situation.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck acknowledges the company’s communication and enclosures.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Manchurian petroleum memorandum
subfiles.about: The note points to a memorandum on petroleum in Japan and Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: It cross-references Hornbeck’s conversation on oil interests and the Manchurian monopoly.

subfiles.title: Note on London military attaché reports
subfiles.about: Reports contain information on Japanese oil and a railway from Harbin.
subfiles.summary: The note flags oil information and the new Harbin–Soviet railway.

subfiles.title: The oil situation
subfiles.about: A cover sheet identifies material concerning the oil situation.
subfiles.summary: The sheet bears the heading “The Oil Situation.”

subfiles.title: Telegram concerning the Sadjira properties
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, for transmission to H. Dundas
subfiles.about: Standard-Vacuum relays confidential news of a Japanese offer for the Sadjira oil properties.
subfiles.summary: The message reports a proposed purchase for one million guilders and requests its relay to company officials.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck relays Sadjira telegram
subfiles.about: The Department passes on Tokyo’s message about the Sadjira properties.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck follows a telephone call with the substance of the embassy telegram requested by Standard-Vacuum.

subfiles.title: Division summary of Tokyo despatch 1207
subfiles.about: The summary describes differing Japanese and foreign views of petroleum reserve requirements.
subfiles.summary: It notes the failure to agree on a joint request for relief, possible Navy opposition, and reports of exploration shifting from Borneo to Taiwan.

subfiles.title: American oil interests in Japan
subfiles.about: Grew reports on talks between Japanese refiners, foreign importers, and government officials.
subfiles.summary: Hashimoto favors a subsidy or higher gasoline prices to pay for reserves, while foreign importers seek a reduction from six months to three. Grew explains why their different commercial positions make joint action difficult. He also reports apparent Army and Navy resistance to easing the rules and Nippon Oil’s interest in Taiwan fields.

subfiles.title: Meeting with Hashimoto at Tokyo Kaikan
subfiles.about: Japanese and foreign company representatives discuss reserves, gasoline prices, and a possible cartel.
subfiles.summary: Hashimoto says Japanese refiners plan to meet reserve requirements but worries about their growing cost; he proposes a subsidy, higher prices, and wider cartel cooperation. Malcolm and Goold favor reducing reserve obligations and separating that issue from pricing. They reserve judgment on any petition or cartel until they see drafts.

subfiles.title: Telegram on anticipated Japanese proposals
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, Tokyo, relaying Walden
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, for H. Dundas
subfiles.about: Company representatives report possible Japanese concessions before the next negotiating session.
subfiles.summary: Godber expects a three-month reserve for importers, protection of current sales, consideration of higher prices, and nondiscrimination, while future growth remains unsettled.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck relays April 8 telegram
subfiles.about: The Department forwards Tokyo’s update on the oil negotiations.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck transmits the embassy’s message and asks that the Texas Company be advised.

subfiles.title: Dundas on the Sadjira concession
subfiles.about: Dundas comments on the Japanese bid for Sadjira.
subfiles.summary: He says prospects for commercial oil are poor and locates the concession on Java near Batavia.

subfiles.title: Dundas thanks Hornbeck for negotiation update
subfiles.about: Dundas responds to news of progress in the oil talks.
subfiles.summary: He welcomes signs of relief from burdensome rules and Hashimoto’s support on shared objections.

subfiles.title: Telegram announcing a provisional understanding
subfiles.about: Grew reports confidential Japanese promises made as the talks conclude.
subfiles.summary: Officials promise future fulfillment of most foreign-company requests; publicity could provoke opposition.

subfiles.title: Telegram outlining April 13 oil understanding
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, Tokyo, relaying Walden and Parker
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, for H. Dundas
subfiles.about: The company representatives detail their understanding with Japanese officials.
subfiles.summary: Officials promise at least 1935 sales volumes, a fair share of future growth, eventual three-month reserve requirements, cost-based prices, and nondiscrimination. The understanding is unsigned, and reducing the legal reserve rule requires other ministries’ approval. The companies defer further storage investment until the rule changes.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck transmits April 15 telegram
subfiles.about: Hornbeck forwards the terms of the reported understanding to Standard-Vacuum.
subfiles.summary: The letter restates the promised quota, reserve, pricing, and nondiscrimination terms and the need to amend the reserve ordinance. It notes that the companies will assess storage investment after the legal change.

subfiles.title: Dundas responds to the April understanding
subfiles.about: Dundas welcomes the reported outcome and offers a later briefing.
subfiles.summary: He expects Walden and Parker to return in May and proposes a fuller discussion then.

subfiles.title: American oil interests in Japan
subfiles.about: Grew reports the return of foreign oil representatives and their negotiating position.
subfiles.summary: The representatives resume talks but refuse further investment under the existing six-month reserve rule. They contemplate cutting sales quotas to match existing storage and consulting headquarters about leaving Japan, hoping the prospect of a gasoline shortage will prompt reconsideration.

subfiles.title: Senate referral of Williams letter
subfiles.about: The Senate refers an enclosed letter for consideration and report.
subfiles.summary: The routing slip requests a report and return of the enclosure.

subfiles.title: Williams proposes a silk-stock requirement
subfiles.about: Williams suggests a reciprocal response to Japan’s oil reserve requirement.
subfiles.summary: He asks whether Japanese silk businesses in the United States could be required to hold comparable stocks.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Connally about Williams’s proposal
subfiles.about: Hull responds to the proposal for a United States silk-stock requirement.
subfiles.summary: Hull says American oil concerns are discussing modification of Japan’s rule with the Japanese Government. He declines further comment on Williams’s proposed response while those talks continue and returns the letter.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch on petroleum-law talks
subfiles.about: The note points to another despatch on talks with Japanese officials.
subfiles.summary: It cross-references a despatch on suspended talks and embassy representations.
